issues.issue: The Auction Agent must deliver notices "after receipt" yet also "at the times and in the manner set forth in the Auction Agreement," two timing standards that need not coincide. Which controls a late delivery is unstated.

The Broker-Dealer Fee Rate "may be adjusted from time to time with the approval of the Company upon a written request of the Broker-Dealer," which is an amendment of a payment term accomplished without the formalities Section 5.6(a) requires — a writing signed by every party and consented to by the Issuer and the Bond Insurer. The two provisions prescribe different routes to changing the same term.

Clause (B) entitles the Broker-Dealer to its fee "if an Auction was not held on such Auction Date," without saying whether an Auction that was held but produced no clearing rate (a failed auction) falls within (A) or (B) or neither. Whether the fee continues to accrue on bonds no owner can sell turns on that undefined distinction.

Item (5) — "if an Auction was not held for any Auction Period, the aggregate principal amount of Outstanding Series 2004 Auction Bonds that were acquired by an Existing Owner through such Broker-Dealer" — is a conditional alternative dropped into a list of cumulative addends joined by "and," so it is unclear whether it is summed with items (1)-(4) or replaces them. The daily-period formula also omits the "of an Existing Owner" qualifier that item (1) carries in Section 2.5(b)'s non-daily formula.

The proviso refers to a Person meeting the requirements "specified in the defmition of 'Broker-Dealer' contained in the Series 2004 Auction Bonds," whereas Section 2.1(c) locates that definition in the Indenture. The mistaken cross-reference leaves the qualification test for a successor Broker-Dealer without an identified source.

The Bond Insurer is given a "right to pay" the fee but the provision states no consequence of its exercise — no discharge of the Company's obligation, no subrogation, and no time within which the right may be exercised. What payment by the Insurer does to the Company's liability under this Section is unaddressed.

BD must "promptly deliver such funds to the party entitled to receive such funds," but the provision never identifies that party and "promptly" sets no deadline. Whether this makes BD a guarantor of a defaulting Potential Owner's payment, and to whom, is exactly what the words leave open.

The exculpation extends to failures to deliver or pay "pursuant to the Auction Procedures or otherwise," a catch-all appended to a specific enumeration that could be read to immunize the Company and Issuer for conduct wholly unrelated to auction settlement. The scope of "or otherwise" has no stated boundary.

The declaration that the Auction Agent "is acting solely as agent of the Trustee" cannot be reconciled with the preamble, which identifies the Trustee as Wells Fargo Bank, National Association — the same entity that is the Auction Agent. An entity cannot meaningfully owe duties solely as agent of itself, and the disclaimer of duties to "any other Person" then sits against the express duties owed to BD in Sections 2.2 and 2.4.

The promise to perform "only such duties as are expressly set forth herein, or expressly incorporated herein by reference pursuant to Section 2.1(b)" is undercut by Section 2.1(b) itself, which incorporates the whole of the Auction Procedures and Settlement Procedures. What counts as an "express" duty once an entire external procedure set is absorbed is left to construction.

The subsection states two different liability standards in consecutive sentences — no liability absent "negligence or misconduct," then no liability for good-faith errors of judgment unless the Agent "shall have been negligent in ascertaining the pertinent facts." "Misconduct" is also unqualified by any willfulness or bad-faith modifier, so its threshold is undefined.

Clause (ii) excuses legal action unless the Auction Agent "has been furnished with indemnity satisfactory to the Auction Agent" — a self-judging standard, and the provision does not say who is obliged to furnish it. The Agent can decline indefinitely on its own assessment.

"Circumstances beyond its reasonable control, including without limitation" is a general phrase followed by an enumeration of catastrophes, raising the ejusdem generis question whether ordinary events — market disruption, a failed auction, a systems vendor's default — qualify. The enumeration is also left grammatically unfinished, ending in a semicolon.

The provision speaks of notice "to the other party" in an agreement among three parties, and makes telecopied notice effective on transmission rather than receipt. Who must be copied, and whether a transmitted but undelivered telecopy is good notice, are both left open.

The clause makes "the other agreements and instruments executed and delivered in connection with the issuance of the Series 2004 Auction Bonds" part of the entire agreement without identifying or limiting them. Which documents are inside the integrated whole — and therefore what the parties may prove — cannot be determined from the words.

The disclaimer of "other representations, endorsements, promises, agreements or understandings, oral, written or inferred" is aimed at Goldman's pre-contract Proposal to Provide Investment Banking Services (November 24, 2003), which touted "unparalleled auction rate performance" and that "our clients' interests always come first." Whether the Proposal survives as part of the parties' bargain or is extinguished by this clause is a direct conflict between the two documents.

Section 5.5 confines enforcement to the Auction Agent, the Bond Insurer and BD and their successors, yet the introductory "NOW, THEREFORE" clause states that BD contracts "for the benefit of the Existing Owners and the Potential Owners of the Series 2004 Auction Bonds." Whether bondholders are intended beneficiaries turns on which of the two passages controls.

The Company is a signatory that pays the Broker-Dealer Fee under Section 2.5 and can direct schedule changes under Section 2.3(a), yet it is omitted from the list of Persons who may enforce the Agreement and from the successors bound. Whether the Company can sue BD on this contract is left in doubt by the omission.

The requirement that no modification or waiver be effective except by a writing signed by every party and consented to by the Issuer and the Bond Insurer conflicts with Section 2.5(a), which lets the Broker-Dealer Fee Rate be adjusted on the Company's approval alone, and with Section 2.3(a), which lets the Auction Agent change the auction schedule at the Company's written direction. Whether those unilateral mechanisms are amendments requiring 5.6(a) formalities is unresolved.

By preserving rights only "with respect to any subsequent breach," the clause carries the negative implication that failure to act does waive the remedy for the breach then occurring. The expressio unius reading is the opposite of what a non-waiver clause is meant to accomplish.

Actions "shall be brought in the United States District Court in the County of New York" names a court that does not exist — there is no federal district court "in the County of New York" by that name — and the clause does not say whether it is exclusive or what happens if federal subject-matter jurisdiction is lacking. The venue designation and the mandatory/permissive character of the clause are both open to construction.

Section 5.10 negates implied duties only "on the part of the Company," while Sections 3.1(a) and 3.1(b) do the same for the Auction Agent; BD alone is left without such protection. Read together, the instrument invites the expressio unius argument that implied duties may be read against BD.
